headline: Our Ancient Ancestor Had One Eye—And It Still Lives in Our Brain
meta_description: Scientists at Lund University reveal vertebrates evolved from a one-eyed creature 600 million years ago, whose median eye survives today as the pineal gland.
summary_short: Researchers discover humans descended from a tiny cyclops-like ancestor that lived nearly 600 million years ago, whose ancient eye still functions in our brains today.
body:
Nearly 600 million years ago, a tiny worm-like creature with a single eye centered on top of its head filtered plankton from the ocean floor—and may have set the stage for every vertebrate eye that followed, including our own. Researchers from Lund University and the University of Sussex now propose that this strange ancestor underwent a remarkable evolutionary journey: it lost its paired eyes when it became sedentary, kept only a simple central eye, then later repurposed that ancient structure to build the sophisticated paired vision system we use today. The discovery upends long-held assumptions about how eyes evolved, revealing that vertebrate eyes developed through an unusual detour rather than a direct path.

What makes this discovery truly remarkable is that the ancient median eye never fully vanished. According to the researchers, it survives today as the pineal gland, a small organ deep in the vertebrate brain. Though the pineal gland no longer helps us see images, it remains profoundly connected to light and darkness, producing melatonin to regulate our sleep cycles and help us wake refreshed each morning.

The findings also explain why our eyes differ so radically from those of insects and squid. In vertebrates, the retina—the light-sensing tissue that powers vision—developed from brain tissue itself, whereas insect and squid eyes evolved from skin cells on the sides of the head. This unusual origin story means our eyes are literally extensions of our brains, a biological legacy stretching back to an ocean-dwelling creature that never could have imagined the world its descendants would eventually see.
quick_facts: Tiny one-eyed ancestor lived in oceans nearly 600 million years ago
Ancient median eye survives today as the human pineal gland
Pineal gland produces melatonin to regulate sleep-wake cycles
Vertebrate retina evolved from brain tissue, unlike insect eyes
Research led by Lund University and University of Sussex
